items.title: Lean and Mathlib Certify a Claude-Assisted Proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
items.summary: On November 20, Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge released a claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library of roughly 17 million lines, saying he developed it with Claude over about six weeks. On November 21 the Lean and Mathlib communities, in a statement endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, said they had 'full confidence' the proof is correct. The check was unusually thorough: dozens of people independently compiled the library (175,187 modules, zero errors), the five headline theorems depend on only the three standard axioms, two comparison tools confirmed it proves Mathlib's own vetted statement rather than a subtly different one, and the exported proof was accepted by Lean's official kernel plus independent checkers including con-leche, con-ron and a Rust kernel. What is not settled: the Clay Institute still lists the problem as unsolved (its prize needs publication and general acceptance), the generalized-Riemann extension was not part of the certification, and no human-readable write-up exists yet - Alpöge jokes the explanation ran past 250,000 pages. Compute cost is reported to be in the millions, a figure he has not confirmed.
items.impact: The lesson is the verification procedure, not the headline. A claim this opaque survived exactly the checks skeptics demanded: correct statement, independent compilation, and checkers that cannot be fooled by a buggy kernel. That is a template for how AI-produced results - in mathematics and increasingly in code - should be judged: machine-checked by independent systems rather than trusted on plausibility. For engineering it points at a future where generated code is certified by proofs, not just spot-checked by tests, and it is the strongest case yet that a frontier model can contribute at the very edge of human knowledge.

items.title: Inside the Team Shipping 11,000 PRs a Month: Fix the Repo, Not AGENTS.md
items.summary: Lauren Tan ('Poteto'), a former Cursor engineer now building Grok Bot, gave a widely circulated talk titled 'All Code Is Slop (Except Mine)' at AI Engineer CODE. Her team delivered about 11,000 PRs in October - over 350 a day - with a revert rate around 0.5%, and she personally shipped roughly 3,000. Her central claim is that AI coding quality is a trust problem, described as an inverted pyramid: put the most weight on the code itself (API design, architecture, refactoring) and deterministic checks (lint, type systems, compiler, tests), and far less on runtime checks, formal methods and natural-language rules. Concretely, her team banned about 99% of code comments after agents copied explanatory comments next to timer-based hacks and the pattern degraded the app; they disabled React's useEffect in product code, allowing it only inside their in-house framework; and when an agent makes the same mistake twice they turn the lesson into a lint rule, a type constraint or a redesigned API rather than adding a line to AGENTS.md. Review has shifted toward verification - screenshots, screen recordings, state diagrams, plus TLA+ model checking, Lean proofs and Bombadil property-based tests. She says roughly 70% of tokens now go to verification, and each release automatically spawns cloud agents that fuzz the app, file fix PRs and even merge them.
items.impact: This is a useful corrective to the reflex of adding more instructions and config when agents misbehave. The argument is that agents faithfully mirror the codebase they are given, so hygiene and machine-enforceable constraints scale while prose rules do not. The uncomfortable part is the endpoint: most product code now lands without deep human review, with trust relocated from review to automated verification. Teams adopting agentic workflows should expect the bottleneck to move from writing code to building the verification harness that makes delegation safe.

items.title: Thinking Machines Ships Inkling 2 Mini: a 20GB Open-Weights Coding Model for a Laptop
items.summary: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini on November 20 with open weights on Hugging Face and inference and fine-tuning on its Tinker platform. It is a mixture-of-experts model with 26.4B total and 3.4B active parameters in roughly 20GB, using a looped transformer that runs its middle layers three times per token (5.4B weight activations per token including looping), natively in NVFP4 with the last four layers in MXFP8. The vendor claims it leads open-weights models under 100B total parameters on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%), acknowledges it trails Qwen3.8-27B on MultiChallenge, and says it compensates for a knowledge gap with search and tool use. In a variable-loop experiment the no-chain-of-thought time horizon grew from 16 seconds at one pass to 37 seconds at three while chain-of-thought stayed legible and sabotage tests did not rise. It was demonstrated offline on a MacBook Pro, with inference support across SGLang, vLLM, Ollama, Unsloth and others. All performance figures are vendor-claimed and were not independently verified.
items.impact: Inkling 2 Mini is a credible local or air-gapped option for coding agents at a size that fits a laptop - relevant when data residency or offline operation rules out hosted models. The looping design adds a useful knob: extra passes buy reasoning time at the cost of latency, which harness engineers can route per task. The caveat is the same one that runs through this week's model releases: the knowledge gap means a production harness must wire in search and tools explicitly, and the benchmarks need rerunning on your own repository before switching.

items.title: A Frontier Model Doubles Dual-Arm Robot Success, Including Shirt-Folding
items.summary: XDOF reported results on November 20 for Ember-0, in which GPT-6.2 Astra directly controls a dual-arm robot across 16 manipulation tasks. Aggregate success rose to 41.2%, nearly double the 19.6% recorded for GPT-6 Astra two months earlier. The standout results were two deformable-object tasks - tying a rope and unfolding a T-shirt - that XDOF says no model had completed in 143 prior valid T-shirt-unfolding trials; a previously hard task, picking up bread with tongs, jumped from 10% to 90%. The experiments ran on six YAM workstations in parallel, 30 repetitions per task, with humans annotating substeps, grasp failures and collisions. Limitations remain clear: the hardware has no tactile feedback, the model must pause to reason between action chunks, and average prediction latency, while down from 15 seconds to 10.1 seconds, is still too slow for real-time correction.
items.impact: This is a useful datapoint on frontier models used as direct robot controllers rather than as high-level planners: general-purpose reasoning is beginning to handle the deformable, open-ended objects that scripted grasping cannot. The gap between lab success and deployment is equally informative - roughly 40% aggregate success, no touch sensing and multi-second action latency mean these are still teleoperated-adjacent trials, not factory-ready autonomy. Watch whether tactile input and faster action chunks close that gap before treating the benchmark jump as a deployment milestone.

items.title: AGIBOT Puts Dozens of Genie G2 Humanoids on an Apple Supplier's Phone Test Line
items.summary: On November 21, AGIBOT announced a strategic partnership with Lens Technology, an Apple supplier, to deploy dozens of Genie G2 humanoid robots on a phone testing line. The robots handle automatic loading and unloading and interact with test equipment across stages such as MMI, antenna and camera testing - repetitive work whose fixtures change quickly with each new phone model. AGIBOT says the general-purpose Genie G2 can work across multiple lines, sharply reducing retooling costs versus fixed automation, can run around the clock to ease labor shortages, and that it has completed the full path from process adaptation and line integration to delivery in a way it can replicate on more lines. The Genie G2 launched last October with an Nvidia Jetson Thor chip, force-controlled arms and 19-degree-of-freedom dexterous hands; in June it livestreamed tablet quality inspection at a Longcheer factory in Nanchang, where AGIBOT claimed a 99.99% success rate. The efficiency and cost claims are the company's own.
items.impact: This is concrete evidence of humanoids moving from demonstration floors into batch industrial deployment, and the choice of task matters: quick-change, high-mix test lines are exactly where fixed automation is expensive to retool, which is a stronger economic case than simple material handling. The broader signal is a split market - general-purpose robots sold on flexibility and replication across lines, versus specialized machines - with the real test being uptime and cost per unit once the novelty of the announcement fades. Treat the headline accuracy figures as vendor claims until independent long-run data appears.
